newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Conference seeks ban on worst child labour abuses.
newsitem.headline: Conference seeks ban on worst child labour abuses.

text.p: The head of the International Labour Organisation said on Wednesday that child labour, which affected up to 250 million children, was no longer defensible and there was a real hope of ending the worst abuses.

"There has been a radical change in attitudes towards the problem," ILO director-General Michel Hansenne told the Amsterdam Child Labour Conference. "We are convinced we can now make a decisive breakthrough."
But India's Labour Minister M. Arunachalam said developing nations needed understanding from Western countries.
"Parents send children away to work instead of sending them to school not because they want it, but because there is no option or alternative for their biological survival," he said.
"To say that children are forcibly sent by parents to work and therefore all working children are forced labour will indeed be a travesty of truth."

The conference, bringing together 200 government ministers, labour union leaders, officials of employer organisations and representatives of working children, drafted a declaration calling for an immediate end to the most extreme forms of child labour.
These included slavery, forced or compulsory labour, and the use of children in prostitution, pornography and the drug trade.

But delegates from developed countries conceded the overall child labour issue was complex and the conference concluded it could not be tackled without wider social programmes in countries where it was common.
"It is essential that we open up the discussion on alternative assistance and support, together with a simultaneous preventive effort," chairman Ad Melkert, the Dutch social affairs minister, said.
ILO chief Hansenne said political and economic changes around the world were bringing real hope of an end to the worst abuses.

He told the conference child labour was no longer internationally accepted as an inevitable consequence of underdevelopment or poverty and the changing world economy was bringing new hope of stopping extreme exploitation.

"The ongoing globalisation of the economy and trade has a beneficial impact on growth and employment, which will provide developing countries with greater resources to reduce the economic necessity of child labour," he said.
The Conference, in its declaration, backed the ILO's ongoing initiative to draft a new convention by 1999 which would oblige its 174 member states to ban extreme forms of child labour.
It also proposed establishing a world-wide monitoring system to track progress and compliance.
Developing nations are deeply suspicious of Western interference in workers rights, fearing this will undermine their main comparative advantage in world trade -- cheap labour.
Some contend that Western nations are using the issue to disguise nascent protectionism and gain unfair trade advantages.

Delegates from developed countries, while conceding the difficulties and complexities of the broader child labour issue, were adamant that immediate action had to be taken against the most extreme forms of exploitation.

"To call these practices 'child labour' is far too mild," German Labour Minister Norbert Blum said. "Bonded labour and debt bondage is slavery. Child prostitution can be murder. You can kill a person's mind and soul as surely as their body."
"The people who take part in these things are swine and they must be stopped."

A background report prepared for the conference says tens of millions of child labourers in South Asia are kept in slavery or under forced labour systems such as debt bondage, where children work to pay off a family obligation.

The report notes the effects of sexual exploitation of children. "Case studies reveal a trauma so deep that many such children are unable to return to a normal life. Many others die before adulthood," it says.
Altogether the ILO says as many as 250 million children in the developing world work, many of them under intolerable conditions.
"We must break this vicious circle in which the working children of today are the illiterate workers of tomorrow, who put their own children to work the day after tomorrow," chairman Melkert said.
